scenes.title: Why is the sky blue?
scenes.narration: Why is the sky blue? The answer is hiding inside sunlight.

scenes.heading: Sunlight looks white
scenes.body: But it is really every colour of the rainbow travelling together.
scenes.narration: Sunlight looks white, but it is really every colour of the rainbow travelling together.

scenes.heading: Each colour is a wave
scenes.body: Red waves are long and lazy. Blue waves are short and choppy.
scenes.narration: Each colour is a wave. Red waves are long and lazy. Blue waves are short and choppy.

scenes.heading: Air scatters short waves
scenes.body: Air molecules bounce short waves in every direction. Long waves mostly pass straight through.
scenes.narration: When sunlight hits the air, tiny molecules bounce the short waves in every direction, while long waves mostly pass straight through.

scenes.label: Blue light scatters about six times more than red
scenes.narration: Blue light scatters about six times more than red. So blue reaches your eyes from every part of the sky.

scenes.heading: Wavelength of light
scenes.narration: Red light has a wavelength near seven hundred nanometres. Blue is around four fifty. Shorter wave, stronger scattering.

scenes.heading: So why not violet?
items: The Sun sends out less violet
Our eyes are less sensitive to it
scenes.narration: Violet scatters even more, so why isn't the sky violet? The Sun sends out less of it, the upper atmosphere absorbs some, and our eyes are less sensitive to it.

scenes.heading: And sunsets?
scenes.body: Light crosses far more air, the blue is scattered away, and red is what is left.
scenes.narration: At sunset, light crosses far more air. The blue gets scattered away, and red is what is left.

scenes.title: Now you know.
scenes.narration: Now you know. Follow for more.
